name: Gosha-jinki-gan (Japanese herbal formula)
short: Case report: lung inflammation (interstitial pneumonia) in a 74-year-old woman. A colon-cancer trial on oxaliplatin was stopped early, with more nerve damage on the formula (51% vs 31%).
text: A 2004 case report describes a 74-year-old woman who developed interstitial pneumonia (fever, dry cough, breathlessness and lung infiltrates on X-ray) after taking gosha-jinki-gan for 5 months for knee pain; she improved after it was stopped, and a lymphocyte stimulation test against the formula was positive. In a placebo-controlled phase III trial in people with colon cancer receiving oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy, the formula was meant to prevent nerve damage (neuropathy), but the trial was stopped at an interim analysis on the safety committee's recommendation: grade 2 or worse neuropathy occurred in 50.6% with the formula and 31.2% with placebo, and use of the formula was significantly associated with neuropathy; in contrast, an open-label randomized trial in 65 people (80% with lung cancer) receiving carboplatin plus paclitaxel found grade 2 or worse neuropathy in 28.1% with the formula and 51.5% in the control arm in its prespecified primary analysis (P = .013), while in an analysis accounting for cancer type and age the estimate still favoured the formula but was attenuated and less precise (hazard ratio 0.48, P = .101); citing the open-label design and this uncertainty, the authors call the findings a phase II signal warranting confirmation in a double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial, and grade 3 to 5 adverse events were similar between arms. In overactive bladder, adverse reactions occurred in 9% of 44 women, and 3 of 30 older men had mild diarrhoea, nausea or urinary frequency; neither abstract describes a comparison group. A laboratory study using human liver cells and liver enzyme preparations found that the formula slowed paclitaxel metabolism only at concentrations much higher than those used clinically, and its authors concluded it does not cause a pharmacokinetic interaction with paclitaxel in practice.
